active_classes.name: retinoid
active_classes.description: Vitamin A derivatives that increase cell turnover

active_classes.name: niacinamide
active_classes.description: Vitamin B3 — barrier support, pore minimizing

active_classes.name: antioxidant
active_classes.description: Free radical protection (vitamin E, ferulic acid …)

active_classes.name: spf
active_classes.description: Sun protection — always the last AM step

active_classes.name: peptide
active_classes.description: Short amino acid chains for collagen support

conflict_rules.reason: Combining retinoids with AHAs in the same routine can cause significant irritation and compromise the skin barrier.
conflict_rules.citation: Draelos ZD. Cosmeceuticals. 2nd ed. Saunders Elsevier; 2009.

conflict_rules.reason: Retinoids and BHAs used together increase risk of over-exfoliation and barrier damage.
conflict_rules.citation: Kligman AM, et al. J Am Acad Dermatol. 1986.

conflict_rules.reason: At high concentrations, vitamin C and niacinamide can form a yellow complex that temporarily reduces efficacy. Modern formulations often mitigate this.
conflict_rules.citation: Zoe Diana Draelos. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2004.

conflict_rules.reason: Benzoyl peroxide oxidizes retinoids, rendering them ineffective.
conflict_rules.citation: Cunliffe WJ, et al. J Dermatolog Treat. 2002.

timing_rules.reason: UV exposure degrades retinoids and increases photosensitivity.
SPF is a daytime protective step only.
AHAs increase photosensitivity; use at night and follow with SPF in AM.
